extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and politically engaged readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (People of the State of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and justifications for structuring executive powers in the proposed U.S. Constitution (term/eligibility, support, veto, commander-in-chief, pardons, treaties, appointments). Useful for judging or designing executive-branch provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility / exclusion from re-eligibility for the chief magistrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments against constitutional rules that exclude a chief magistrate from serving again (perpetual or partial exclusion). Hamilton examines the ill effects of exclusion of a man from serving his country again by the choice of his fellowcitizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disadvantages listed include: (1) a man at the summit tempted to embrace a favorable conjuncture to prolong power by personal hazard; (2) deprives the community of experience gained by the chief magistrate ('That experience is the parent of wisdom'); (3) banishes men from stations where they might be essential in emergencies (war or crisis); (4) operates as an interdiction of stability in the administration, 'necessitating a mutability of measures'; (5) even partial exclusion makes readmission remote and precarious. Claimed advantages (greater independence/security) are rebutted: limited or speculative and can produce perverse incentives (public disgust, fomenting danger). Conclusion: avoid self-denying perpetual exclusion; allow re-election/readmission to preserve experience, stability, and the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate provision for the executive's support (compensation protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President 'shall, at stated times, receive for his services a compensation WHICH SHALL NEITHER BE INCREASED NOR DIMINISHED DURING THE PERIOD FOR WHICH HE SHALL HAVE BEEN ELECTED; and he SHALL NOT RECEIVE WITHIN THAT PERIOD ANY OTHER EMOLUMENT from the United States, or any of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Legislative control over salary would make the executive 'obsequious' to the legislature via distress or largess; power over a man's support is a power over his will. Fixing compensation for the term prevents weakening fortitude by operating on necessities or corrupting integrity by appealing to avarice. Examples/anti-patterns: leaving salary at legislative discretion invites intimidation or seduction of the Executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each branch must have constitutional arms / competent powers for self-defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of powers requires furnishing each department with constitutional arms for its own defense; a mere parchment delineation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Without constitutional means of self-defense, one branch (legislature) could intrude upon or absorb the powers of others. The executive needs powers (e.g., the veto) not because he is presumed superior in wisdom, but because the legislature is not infallible and may err by faction, haste, or encroachment. Guidance for designers: supply effectual defensive powers to preserve the balance among branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive veto power (qualified negative) on legislative acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The President should possess a qualified negative: power of returning bills with objections so they do not become laws unless ratified by two thirds of each house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions: (a) shield the Executive against legislative encroachment; (b) furnish additional security against enaction of improper laws by checking faction, precipitancy, or impulses unfriendly to the public good. Preference for qualified over absolute negative: a qualified negative (return for reconsideration, override only by two-thirds) is less harsh, more likely to be exercised, encourages deliberation, and combines Executive objections with a respectable proportion of the legislature. Anticipated behavior: the veto will be used sparingly; the danger is more likely non-use than overuse. Anti-pattern: withholding a veto power leaves the Executive unable to defend itself; an absolute negative may be unnecessarily abrasive and less likely to be exercised prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design the veto so override thresholds balance activity vs. minority obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Require a supermajority (two thirds) of each legislative chamber to override an Executive veto, applied to two-thirds of members present rather than two-thirds of all members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Requiring more than a majority for resolution tends to embarrass government operations and subject majority to minority. Two-thirds of members present reduces paralysis (avoids de facto unanimity due to absences), promotes punctual attendance, and preserves activity of public councils. Examples cited: states of paralysis under rules requiring unanimity (Roman Tribuneship, Polish Diet, States-General) are to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the judiciary distinct and insulated from executive political functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should not be placed in positions that create bias or political entanglement (e.g., serving habitually in an executive council that revises legislation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: If judges give prior opinions in a revisionary capacity or are often associated with the Executive, they might be induced to embark too far in the political views of the magistrate and form a dangerous combination between executive and judiciary. 'It is impossible to keep the judges too distinct from every other avocation than that of expounding the laws.' Anti-pattern: integrating judges into executive councils risks corruption or undue influence and compromises judicial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive as commander-in-chief of military and naval forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The President should be 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States WHEN CALLED INTO THE ACTUAL SERVICE of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Direction of war demands qualities suited to a single hand: direction of the common strength, unity of direction, decision, secrecy, and dispatch. Precedent: most state constitutions concentrate military authority in the chief magistrate. Anti-pattern: diffusing military command among many is unsuited to the necessities of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential power to require written opinions of principal executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each executive department upon any subject relating to their duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary: Hamilton regards this as somewhat redundant (the right arises from the office itself) but affirms the practice. Use: fosters informed executive decision-making; no further special restrictions suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power vested in the President (except in cases of impeachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is authorized to grant 'reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, EXCEPT IN CASES OF IMPEACHMENT.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: The pardoning power allows humane exceptions to the severity of criminal law and should be as little fettered as possible. A single magistrate is argued to be better fitted to weigh delicate motives for mercy and to act quickly in crises. Exception discussion: for treason some argue legislative concurrence may be appropriate, but counterarguments stress the necessity of rapid discretionary clemency in rebellions/insurrections (timeliness can be decisive). Anti-patterns: making pardons subject to slow legislative concurrence may foreclose timely offers that restore public tranquillity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making: President acts 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate' (two-thirds present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties should be made by the President 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Treaty-making is sui generis (partly legislative, partly executive) and suits joint participation by Executive and a portion of the legislature. Objections to sole-executive or Senate-alone power: sole executive risks corruption (an elective short-term magistrate may be tempted by foreign inducement); Senate-alone would lose benefits of constitutional agency and confidence of foreign powers. Excluding the House is defended: House's fluctuating, numerous composition, lack of secrecy and dispatch, and greater calls on its time make it ill-suited. Two-thirds of present members is preferred over two-thirds of all members to avoid practical unanimity requirements, encourage punctual attendance, and prevent paralysis; requiring a fixed number of all members would diminish incentives to attend and risk impotence and disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment power: President nominates with Senate advice and consent; Congress may vest inferior appointments; recess appointments permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The President 'to NOMINATE, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution.' Congress may by law vest appointment of inferior officers elsewhere. The President may fill vacancies during the recess of the Senate by granting commissions which expire at the end of their next session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: This mode is presented as well calculated to promote judicious choice of persons to fill offices — 'the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration.' Options for vesting appointment (single man; select assembly; or man with concurrence of assembly) are recognized; the chosen scheme (President with Senate concurrence) balances executive initiative and legislative check. Recess appointment provision ensures continued administration between sessions. Antipattern: vesting all appointment power in a single body without checks risks poor selection or politicization; allowing Congress unfettered removal or appointment control would undermine administrative independence.
